title: The Heavier Coin
problem: Nine visually identical coins include exactly one heavier counterfeit coin. Using a balance scale only twice, identify the counterfeit coin.

hints.text: Each weighing has three possible outcomes, so divide the candidates into three equally sized groups.
Weigh three coins against three coins, then use the second weighing within the indicated group of three.

solution.setup: Split the coins into groups A, B, and C of three coins each. Weigh A against B.
solution.reasoning: If A and B balance, the heavy coin is in C. If they do not, it is in the heavier group. In either case exactly three candidates remain. Weigh one candidate against a second: if they balance, the third is counterfeit; otherwise the heavier weighed coin is counterfeit.
solution.finalAnswer: Two weighings are sufficient using a 3-3-3 split followed by a 1-versus-1 comparison.
solution.sanityCheck: Two balance-scale weighings have at most 3^2=9 outcome paths, exactly enough to distinguish nine equally possible candidates.

keyInsight: Design each observation to divide the remaining possibilities as evenly as its possible outcomes allow.
recognitionCues: A limited-query identification problem suggests measuring information and building a balanced decision tree.
commonMistakes: Beginning with a 4-versus-4 weighing, whose unbalanced result leaves four candidates that one weighing cannot always distinguish.
followUps: How many coins can three weighings handle when the counterfeit is known to be heavier?

source.notes: Original wording of a classic balance-scale information problem.

verification.notes: The explicit strategy resolves all nine cases, matching the information lower bound.
